parts.title: Sentence Reading
teacherDirections: Read each of the ten source sentences silently and then aloud. Use the paired teacher-created weave question to vary attention to concept, structure, vocabulary, phrasing, and meaning.

sentences: Mike and Ella hung the new television on the wall above the fireplace.
The collision resulted in a big dent in the front end of the van.
The suspension bridge was made with extra strong cables.
Half the shoreline is missing because of the erosion.
Lena and Jack found themselves in a state of confusion during math class.
The whole class got an extension for the earth science project.
There is a lot of national pride on this special occasion.
Brandy could sense a lot of tension between Tom and Ellen.
We must finish the conclusion of the book ourselves.
I am upset about this invasion of stink bugs!
weaveQuestions: In television, what sound does sion represent?
How many syllables do you hear in collision, and where is the final stable syllable?
What does suspension describe in this sentence?
What caused the shoreline to change?
Which High Frequency Word refers back to Lena and Jack?
What does extension mean in the earth science sentence?
Read the national-pride sentence with natural phrasing. Where would you scoop?
What feeling does tension name in this sentence?
Which word carries the /zhən/ sound in the conclusion sentence?
Explain the meaning of invasion in the final sentence.

parts.title: Passage Reading
teacherDirections: Read the complete controlled passage. Passage history is explicitly unverified, so confirm it has not already been completed before using it. Ask all ten teacher-created questions in the required ladder.

data.passage:
Mr. Vincent wants to plan a celebration for his whole class of first-grade students. It will be a special occasion for the end of the school year!

The students have come a long way since the first day of school. Back then, half of the students did not use capitalization in their compositions. Today, they know to use a capital for the first word in a sentence and with a specific name, place, or thing. The students have finished hundreds of books in total, putting their well-developed reading skills to the test.

On top of all of that, the students have their addition and subtraction facts down pat in math. They are also good at communication, active discussions, asking questions that make sense, and using their imaginations to solve tricky problems. Mr. Vincent is so pleased with their progress and, best of all, the kids are pleased with themselves.

For the big celebration, Mr. Vincent will get a bunch of decorations, vanilla cupcakes, and plenty of drinks. He plans to have music, crafts, and games as well. Mr. Vincent is envisioning a great time for all!

Mr. Vincent thinks that one student’s suggestion to extend invitations to the school administration and the students’ families is great. He hopes the celebration will be a hit with all who attend. He is so glad that he will be able to demonstrate to his students how accomplished they are before they set off on vacation - and then on to second grade!
data.historyNote: Current records do not establish the next unread 7.4 passage. This passage follows the source sequence provisionally; repeat the last unread passage instead if classroom history shows otherwise.

questions.question: What occasion is the celebration for?
What capitalization skill do the students now know?
Name two school skills the passage says the students have developed.
Why is Mr. Vincent pleased with the students?
How are the students’ academic progress and the planned celebration connected?
Explain why Mr. Vincent likes the suggestion to invite families and the administration.
What can you infer about how the students feel about their own progress?
Which details best show how much the class has grown since the start of school?
How does the celebration recognize both the students’ work and their transition to second grade?
